edges.description: Aspirated oral and upper-airway material seeds the lower respiratory tract with mixed anaerobic and aerobic flora.
In model systems, Prevotella products increase lower-airway bacterial adhesion, suggesting one mechanism by which oral anaerobes can amplify coinfecting bacterial pneumonia.
Mixed anaerobic-aerobic infection in the lung can produce systemic febrile illness.
Higher lower-airway bacterial adhesion can increase the lung bacterial burden that drives host cytokine release.
Sustained mixed bacterial growth and cytokine-rich inflammation are upstream of the tissue destruction that distinguishes cavitary anaerobic disease from uncomplicated pneumonia.
Necrotizing anaerobic pneumonia destroys lung parenchyma and forms cavitary pulmonary abscesses.
Cavitary anaerobic disease can drain foul, putrid material into the airway and cause productive cough.
Peripheral or ruptured cavitary infection can extend through the pleura, creating empyema or bronchopleural fistula.
Cavitary lung abscess can erode inflamed airway and vascular tissue, producing hemoptysis in some anaerobic abscess presentations.
Cavitary and pleural inflammation can manifest with chest pain.
Pleural extension seeds infected fluid in the pleural cavity and produces empyema.
Loss of ordinary airway protection permits aspiration, the initiating event for anaerobe-dominant primary lung abscess.
Impaired swallowing and cough clearance make inhalation of oropharyngeal secretions into alveoli more likely.
